title: Metal-free sampling methods for environmental analysis
author: Noernberg, Bujaczek, et al.
materials: Furthermore, a plastic tool 58 cm in length was developed to remove the sediment sample in the acrylic tubing from the corer into separate bottles (Figs. 10; 11). The tool can also be used to push the acrylic tubing out of the corer (Figs. 10; 11). The plastic tool features a square plastic end piece with the square portion measuring 1.0 × 4.4 × 4.4 cm (Fig. 11). The four corners of the square end piece tapers down to form a cylinder (3.0 × 0.4 × 4 cm) that is pushed onto carbon fibre tubing (Fig. 11). On the opposite end of the tool is a circular plastic end piece (5.8 cm in length), with the larger circular portion measuring 1.4 × 3.2 × 3.2 cm (Fig. 4). This end serves as the handle, and tapers into a narrower cylinder (Fig. 11). To remove the sediment from the sampler, the sediment corer must first be disassembled from the carbon fiber pole, leaving the circular end of the corer open (Figs. 8; 10). The square end piece is inserted into the tapered 4.2 × 4.2 cm square end of the sediment corer and the plastic tool is used to push the sediment out towards the circular end of the corer (Figs. 8a; 11). Using clean sampling and handling methods [42], the sediment sample is pushed from the corer and emptied into plastic bottles. Alternatively, the sediment can be stored in the acrylic tubing. Two square PP pieces (4.5 × 4.5 × 0.5 cm) can be inserted inside the acrylic tubing to prevent the sample from shifting during transport and is wrapped with plastic wrap (Fig. 9d).Fig. 11Square tool used for removing acrylic tubing housing a sediment sample from the lake sediment corer.Fig 11:

Using metal-free sampling equipment that has been cleaned in high purity acid allows the greatest risks of TE contamination to be effectively eliminated or at least dramatically reduced [2,4,11,15,17,[19], [20], [21],[23], [24], [25]. All of the equipment described here has been shown to function properly for its intended application. However, some disadvantages exist and need to be acknowledged. Firstly, the majority of the metal-free sampling equipment described here were fabricated using PETG and PP. Unlike the metal alloys used in many sampling devices, these 3-D printed materials are not durable and are prone to breakage if not handled with care. Cold weather amplifies this problem, as it was observed that certain plastic sampling devices became more brittle when exposed to freezing temperatures. For example, the sediment corer was used during winter sampling, and freezing would occur around the 316 stainless steel threads (Fig. 8b). After repeated sampling, water freezing around the threads caused the plastic to be more brittle and would crack, which presented a problem in ensuring the sampler was properly secured to the pole. Secondly, any of the equipment mounted on aluminum poles (e.g. the rain and dust collectors) must be securely fixed to the ground with ropes and tent pegs (Figs. 1; 3). High winds can cause the rain and dust collectors to dislodge from the pole and result in damage if they are not secured properly. Thirdly, carbon fibre tubing used for the sediment corer and plant collectors is lightweight, but not indestructible; during sediment coring, cracking around the holes connecting the carbon fibre tubing segments was observed when sampled from a watercraft. It is advisable to purchase high quality carbon fibre tubing for this device, and that the sediment corer and plant collector are handled with care. And lastly, the sediment corer is ideal for fine-grained sediments, but certainly not for gravel or cobbles. Small rocks and pebbles create difficulty in attaining a sediment core as these obstacles prevent the corer from easily descending into the sediment. The corer must be handled with care in these conditions, or the plastic will crack.

steps.title: Design and fabricate components
steps.instruction: Use Fusion 360 to design each plastic part, print prototypes in PLA and final parts in PET, PETG, PP, PC or PC‑CF; print threaded holes when possible; fabricate metal parts from aluminum alloy or 316 stainless steel for rigidity.

steps.title: Assemble Aeolian Frisbee dust collector
steps.instruction: Print the deflector ring (62.3 cm diam × 9.8 cm h) and outer ring (OD 64.5 cm, ID 38.5 cm) in PETG; print the central mount (29.9 cm diam × 3.0 cm h, wall 0.25 cm) and stabilize it with eight PETG spokes (3.3 × 6.2 × 3.0 cm) using epoxy; drill four 8.0 cm‑radius holes in the mount base; print the removable collecting bowl (29.7 cm diam × 3.0 cm h, wall 0.1 cm) and fill with two layers of 1.6 cm PP balls; place a circular grid (29.7 cm diam × 2.0 cm h, wall 0.2 cm) over the balls; add a lid (30 cm diam × 1.0 cm h, wall 0.2 cm) for rain; mount an aluminum pole (inner hole 1.5 cm, outer 3.0 cm) through the lower hole of the deflector ring; attach four rectangular PETG pieces (2.9 × 5.5 × 0.5 cm) with 0.5 cm holes for ropes and secure the whole assembly to the ground with ropes/pegs.

steps.title: Construct metal‑free moss boxes
steps.instruction: Cut two PETG grids (20 × 20 × 1 cm) with 0.6 cm mesh; assemble as top and bottom halves; secure the four corners with plastic cable ties.

steps.title: Fabricate moisture‑activated rain collector
steps.instruction: Print six PETG parts: (a) funnel (18.5 × 22.8 × 22.8 cm) epoxy‑glued to a platform (17.0 × 8.4 × 2.4 cm) that holds a hollow cylinder (3.0 × 3.0 × 3.0 cm) for a 20.6 × 1.3 × 1.3 cm aluminum pole; (b) lid (22.8 cm diam × 1.0 cm h) mounted on a 16.0 × 2.0 × 1.0 cm stand; (c) 500 mL PP bottle cap; (d) plastic cylinder (6.0 × 2.5 × 2.5 cm) with three wings (6.0 × 2.0 × 0.6 cm) each having a 1 cm hole; (e) circular platform (5.4 × 5.4 × 0.8 cm) for a 2 m aluminum pole; (f) power system: 42 × 32 cm solar panel on two poles (45°), PWM solar charge controller (LS1012EU 10A 12 V), 12 V 10 A relay module (F‑1020), Dakota Lithium 12B 10 Ah LiFePO₄ battery in a waterproof Pelican case; mount the Hydreon Optical Solid State Rain Gauge RG‑9 sensor on the stand; connect sensor to relay and controller.

steps.title: Operate rain collector
steps.instruction: When the sensor detects rain, its infrared beam is interrupted, triggering the relay to swing the lid 180° open; a timer keeps the lid open 15 min after rain stops, then closes it; rain flows through the funnel, exits a 3.6 cm hole at the narrow end, travels through a 45°‑angled channel to an acid‑cleaned PP collection bottle (up to 1 L) whose lid rests on a 5.6 × 5.6 × 0.3 cm ledge; epoxy glue and 316 SS screws never contact the water.

steps.title: Assemble water column sampler
steps.instruction: Print two identical wheels (32.5 × 32.5 × 0.4 cm) each with three 1 cm holes; attach them to a smaller wheel (27.5 cm diam × 0.4 cm h) to create a 5 cm channel for acid‑cleaned PE tubing; mount the wheel assembly on a stand (29 × 3.0 × 4.0 cm) resting on two plastic cylinders (11.7 × 4.0 × 4.0 cm); drill a 1 cm hole in the back of the wheel, feed PE tubing through this hole, through the central holes on both sides, and out the front where it connects via clean‑room fittings to a collection‑bottle lid (1 cm hole); attach a second short PE segment to the lid; create vacuum with a peristaltic pump to draw water; lower the tubing by pushing the hollow handle (5.1 × 2.8 cm) attached to a rod (5.8 × 2.8 cm) on a circular platform (4.0 cm diam × 0.8 cm); use a 316 SS weight encased in PP layers to keep tubing from floating; limit depth with a pole‑handle (14 × 3.4 cm) inserted through the wheel holes; PE tubing length around the wheel is 6 m (extendable).

steps.title: Build SWAMP Lab “Fish” torpedo sampler
steps.instruction: 3‑D print a solid PP rod (10.5 × 8.0 × 8.0 cm) and turn it on a lathe into a cone; drill a 0.6 cm hole through the dorsal side to the tip; thread acid‑cleaned PE tubing through the hole, extending 5 mm past the nose tip; fit the nose cone into a 316 SS cylinder (27.5 × 8.0 × 8.0 cm) that carries two horizontal fins (10.1 × 6.0 × 0.3 cm) and one vertical fin (8.8 × 0.3 × 2.5 cm) with four 1 cm holes; attach a larger fin (28.1 × 0.3 × 32.0 cm) perpendicular to flow and a smaller fin (17.7 × 4.4 × 0.3 cm) parallel to the bottom; bolt five 11.5 cm perforated 316 SS strips to the large fin with 316 SS screws, securing PE tubing with a cable tie; adjust strip angle to level the sampler in current; deploy from a boat, orient the nose upstream, and sample with a peristaltic pump into an acid‑cleaned bottle.

steps.title: Construct laminar‑flow growth chamber
steps.instruction: Cut three vinyl sheets (132 × 125 × 95 cm) and attach them to an anodized 6560 Al frame (134 × 131 × 100 cm); seal the opening with a flexible vinyl cover fastened with double‑sided tape and Velcro for access; install an air‑handling unit with adjustable flow feeding a Technical Air Products HEPA filter mounted on top of the chamber; verify laminar flow from the top onto the grated table using a Lighthouse 3016 IAQ laser particle counter.

steps.title: Assemble submerged aquatic plant sampler
steps.instruction: Print PETG handle top and bottom squares (14.9 × 14.9 × 4 cm) and secure them with 18 stainless‑steel screws, leaving a central 11 × 11 cm opening; insert a narrower PETG handle (11 × 1 × 1.8 cm) into the opening and secure to an aluminum pole with a stainless screw; attach the pole to a carbon‑fiber pole made of two 50.3 cm sections epoxy‑glued to aluminum poles; construct the cutting end: a rectangular PETG piece (46 × 3.6 × 4.3 cm) encasing the carbon‑fiber pole (2 cm diam); attach a diamond‑shaped PETG piece (7.6 × 2.5 × 2.6 cm) at 45° holding zirconium‑dioxide blades (4.1 × 1.0 cm) that fit into two 1 cm slits on the rectangle; when the handle is lowered, the blades swing 3.5 cm outward, exposing the opening; closing the handle pushes the blades back and cuts the plant; secure blades with two curved PETG pieces (4.5 × 0.4 × 2.4 cm).

steps.title: Fabricate metal‑free lake sediment corer
steps.instruction: 3‑D print a PETG corer (36 × 5.2 × 5.2 cm, 0.3 cm thick) with a square opening 4.2 × 4.2 × 0.3 cm that widens to 5.2 cm over 3 cm; add a 0.5 cm platform and a hollow square casing (5.2 × 5.2 × 0.5 cm); attach a PP door (5.2 × 5.2 × 0.5 cm) with hinged PP segments (4.3 × 2.0 × 0.5 cm) that open only outward; load acrylic tubing (33.5 × 5.7 × 5.2 cm) from the opposite end, resting on the platform; include four 14 cm tapered windows on the sides for visual inspection; mount a circular platform (8.0 × 8.0 × 1.0 cm) with four stainless‑steel threads (1.7 × 1.7 × 1.0 cm) and attach to a sampling pole via stainless screws; the pole has a plastic attachment (12 × 8.0 × 0.4 cm) tapered at 45° in four directions forming a cylinder (8.0 × 0.4 × 2.9 cm); drill a 0.6 cm hole perpendicular to the cylinder for a carbon‑fiber tube (2 cm diam) and secure with a stainless screw; extend depth (1–5 m) by adding carbon‑fiber segments joined with stainless cotter pins.

steps.title: Use sediment corer removal tool
steps.instruction: Print a 58 cm plastic tool: square end (1.0 × 4.4 × 4.4 cm) tapering to a cylinder (3.0 × 0.4 × 4 cm); opposite circular end (5.8 cm length, 1.4 × 3.2 × 3.2 cm) tapering to a handle; after coring, detach the corer from the pole, insert the square end into the corer’s 4.2 × 4.2 cm opening and push the sediment toward the circular end; transfer sediment into clean plastic bottles or leave in the acrylic tubing; optionally place two PP pieces (4.5 × 4.5 × 0.5 cm) inside the tubing and wrap with plastic film for transport.

steps.title: Validate metal‑free status of devices
steps.instruction: Cut a 5 cm strand (~150 mg) of each plastic material; clean according to the SWAMP laboratory plastic‑ware protocol; leach each strand in 10 mL of 2 % nitric acid (sub‑boiled, pH < 1) for 24 h; analyze leachates for ~40 trace elements by ICP‑MS (ThermoFisher iCAP Qc) in the metal‑free ultraclean SWAMP lab.

description: All of the plastic materials used in our laboratory and described herein are subjected to simple leaching tests to identify any anomalous concentrations of TEs. Specifically, a 5 cm strand of each plastic weighing approximately 150 mg is cleaned using our routine SWAMP laboratory cleaning procedure for plasticware [46], then leached for 24 h in 10 ml of 2% nitric acid; the acid is purified twice by sub-boiling distillation in a quartz still (Duopur, MLS, Leutkirch, Germany). Leachates are analyzed for approximately 40 TEs using ICP-MS (iCAP Qc, ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Cleaning, leaching, and analysis all takes place in the metal-free, ultraclean, SWAMP laboratory. These leaching conditions are extremely corrosive (pH < 1), in contrast to the pH range of most natural waters (pH 4 to 8). We do not follow any of the diverse, commonly used, standardized methods for quantifying element migration, extraction, or leaching (see [55], for a review). However, the purpose of our tests is simply to identify whether there are anomalous concentrations of individual TEs in the plastics that might contribute significantly to blank concentrations. Examples of such anomalous element releases include leaching of Pb from LDPE, Sb from PET, V from HDPE, or Zn from rubber (Table S2). Metal-free devices help to mitigate TE contamination risks when sampling dust, rainwater, surface waters, plants, and sediments. Our laboratory has been able to construct metal-free devices that are not available through commercial means while providing invaluable innovations for environmental TE research. Metal-free devices allows researchers to mitigate a major source of contamination: sample collection. The use of metal-free equipment helps to reduce TE blank values, thereby improving analytical sensitivity, accuracy and precision.
